questions.title: Function of a bacterial plasmid
questions.question: The functions of plasmid are?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plasmid is a small, circular, extrachromosomal DNA molecule that can replicate itself, but "DNA replication" as a generic cellular process is not what the plasmid does for the cell -- it is not the bacterial chromosome's own replication machinery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes reading messenger RNA; a plasmid is DNA, not a protein-synthesis apparatus, though it may carry genes that are later transcribed and translated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cell wall synthesis is directed by chromosomally encoded genes and enzymes (e.g. those building peptidoglycan); it is not a function carried out by a plasmid.
explanations.D: Correct. A plasmid is a small circular extrachromosomal DNA molecule that typically carries accessory genes -- most classically antibiotic-resistance or virulence genes -- rather than performing any of the three listed cellular processes itself. None of DNA replication (of the chromosome), protein synthesis, or cell wall synthesis describes what a plasmid actually is or does; it is best understood as an accessory genetic element the cell carries, not a functional apparatus for these core processes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a plasmid as a small circular extrachromosomal DNA molecule carrying accessory genes, distinct from the chromosome's own replication, protein synthesis or cell-wall-synthesis machinery.

questions.title: Clone: a population from a single cell
questions.question: A population of cells derived from a single cell are called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Monoclonal" is the adjective describing something derived from a single clone (e.g. a monoclonal antibody); it is not the standard noun used for the population itself.
explanations.B: Correct. A clone is the population of genetically identical cells produced when a single parent cell divides repeatedly -- ordinary cell division (binary fission in bacteria) does not introduce new genetic variation, so every descendant remains identical to the original cell. "Clone" names this population directly, which is why it is the term tested here rather than the adjective "monoclonal." This vocabulary underlies later concepts such as monoclonal antibodies, which are themselves the product of one such clone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A protoplast is a bacterial cell that has had its cell wall removed (e.g. by lysozyme), leaving only the membrane-bound cell -- an unrelated concept to a population derived from one ancestor cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A subculture is the transfer of cells from one growth medium to fresh medium to maintain or expand a culture; it describes a laboratory technique, not the genetic relationship among the cells produced from a single ancestor.

questions.learning_objective: Identify "clone" as the term for a population of cells derived from one parent cell, distinguishing it from protoplast and subculture.

questions.title: Gram-negative bacteria: stain colour
questions.question: Gram negative bacteria appear as?

explanations.A: Correct. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer lipid membrane; the decolourising step (alcohol/acetone) disrupts this thin wall and washes out the crystal violet-iodine complex, so the cell instead takes up the safranin counterstain and appears pink/red under the microscope. This colour is a direct, mechanistic readout of the thin Gram-negative wall, not an arbitrary label. It is the opposite result from Gram-positive organisms, whose thick wall retains the primary stain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Violet is the colour produced by a thick peptidoglycan wall retaining the crystal violet-iodine complex -- the Gram-positive result, not the Gram-negative one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A Gram-negative cell shows only one colour (pink/red) on a correctly performed Gram stain, not both -- the two colours correspond to two mutually exclusive wall types.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gram-negative bacteria do reliably produce a colour on Gram stain (pink/red); "none of these" is only correct if the true answer is absent from the list, which it is not.

questions.learning_objective: State that Gram-negative bacteria stain pink/red on Gram stain, because their thin wall fails to retain the crystal violet primary stain.

questions.title: Gram-positive bacteria: stain colour
questions.question: Gram positive bacteria appear as?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pink/red is the colour produced when the primary stain washes out of a thin wall and the safranin counterstain takes over -- the Gram-negative result, not the Gram-positive one.
explanations.B: Correct. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that traps the crystal violet-iodine complex through the decolourisation step, so the cell retains the primary stain and appears violet/purple under the microscope. This colour is a direct consequence of wall thickness: the thicker the peptidoglycan mesh, the more effectively it holds the dye complex in place against the decolouriser. It is the opposite result from Gram-negative organisms, whose thin wall and outer lipid membrane let the primary stain wash out.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A Gram-positive cell shows only one colour (violet/purple) on a correctly performed Gram stain, not both.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gram-positive bacteria do reliably produce a colour on Gram stain (violet/purple); "none of these" is only correct if the true answer is absent from the list, which it is not.

questions.learning_objective: State that Gram-positive bacteria stain violet/purple on Gram stain, because their thick wall retains the crystal violet primary stain.

questions.title: Eukaryotic vs prokaryotic cells: the false statement
questions.question: Differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells include all of the following EXCEPT?

options.B: Prokaryotic cells division by binary fission
options.C: Eukaryotic cells have cilia and flagella with complex structure
options.D: Prokaryotic cells have no genetic material

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is true, so it is not the EXCEPT answer). Eukaryotic cells do have membrane-bound mitochondria; prokaryotic cells lack this organelle entirely -- a genuine difference between the two cell types.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Prokaryotic cells do divide by binary fission, a simple splitting of one cell into two identical daughters, unlike the mitotic division of eukaryotic cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Where present, eukaryotic flagella and cilia have a complex internal "9+2" microtubule structure, unlike the simpler flagellin-filament flagella of bacteria -- a genuine structural difference.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. A prokaryotic cell does have genetic material -- a single circular chromosome of DNA -- it simply lacks a membrane-bound nucleus to enclose it, holding the DNA instead in an unbound cytoplasmic region called the nucleoid. "No genetic material" would mean no DNA at all, which is not true of any living bacterial cell.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish genuine eukaryote-vs-prokaryote differences (mitochondria, binary fission, flagellar/ciliary complexity) from the false claim that prokaryotes lack genetic material altogether.

questions.title: A true statement about prokaryotes
questions.question: Which statement is true about prokaryotes?

options.C: They usually lack a cell wall
options.E: They contain a single circular DNA molecule as the genetic material

explanations.A: Incorrect. Prokaryotes specifically lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus -- their DNA sits in an unbound cytoplasmic nucleoid region instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mitochondria are a eukaryotic membrane-bound organelle; prokaryotic cells have no mitochondria at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Most prokaryotes (bacteria) typically do have a cell wall (peptidoglycan-based); only exceptions such as Mycoplasma naturally lack one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prokaryotes divide by binary fission, a simple splitting process, not by mitosis, which is a eukaryotic process involving a mitotic spindle and chromosome segregation.
explanations.E: Correct. The defining genetic feature of a prokaryotic cell is that its entire genome is typically carried on a single circular DNA chromosome, held free in the cytoplasm (the nucleoid) rather than enclosed by a nuclear membrane. This single-circular-chromosome arrangement, together with the absence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, is what makes a cell prokaryotic rather than eukaryotic.

questions.learning_objective: State that a prokaryote's genetic material is a single circular DNA chromosome, and reject the eukaryotic features (nucleus, mitochondria, mitosis) and the false wall-absence claim.

questions.title: Prokaryotic cells: characteristic features
questions.question: Prokaryotic cells are characterized by?

options.A: The lack of an organized nucleus
options.B: Cells that can move by flagella
options.C: The lack of membrane bound organelles

explanations.A: Incorrect alone (this statement is true but only part of the answer). Prokaryotic cells do lack an organized, membrane-bound nucleus, but this is only one of several defining features asked about here, not the complete answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Many prokaryotic cells do move by flagella, but motility is only one of the listed features, not the complete answer by itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Prokaryotic cells do lack membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi), but this too is only one of the listed features.
explanations.D: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Prokaryotic cells typically do have a cell wall, but this is again only one feature among several, not the complete answer.
explanations.E: Correct. Each of the four preceding statements -- lack of an organized nucleus, motility by flagella (in motile species), lack of membrane-bound organelles, and typically having a cell wall -- is individually a true characteristic of prokaryotic cells. Since the question asks what characterizes prokaryotic cells and every listed option is a genuine, standard feature, "all of the above" is the composite correct answer rather than any single item alone.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that lack of an organized nucleus, flagellar motility, lack of membrane-bound organelles and typically having a cell wall are all standard prokaryotic features, jointly rather than individually.

questions.title: Peritrichous flagellar arrangement
questions.question: When flagella are distributed all around a bacterial cell, the arrangement is called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Polar" describes flagella confined to one or both poles (as in monotrichous, amphitrichous or lophotrichous arrangements), the opposite of flagella distributed all around the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Random" is not a recognised flagellar-arrangement term; the all-around distribution described here has its own specific name.
explanations.C: Correct. Peritrichous describes flagella distributed all around the bacterial cell surface, not confined to one or two poles -- Escherichia coli is a classic peritrichous example. This distinguishes it from the three polar arrangements (monotrichous, amphitrichous, lophotrichous), which all confine flagella to one or both poles of the cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Encapsulated" describes a bacterium with a capsule (an outer polysaccharide layer), an entirely different structure unrelated to flagellar arrangement.

questions.learning_objective: Name "peritrichous" as the term for flagella distributed all around a bacterial cell, distinct from the three polar arrangements and from capsule terminology.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Monotrichous flagellar arrangement
questions.question: One flagellum at one end of the organism is called?

explanations.A: Correct. Monotrichous (monotrichate) describes a single flagellum located at one pole of the bacterial cell -- Vibrio cholerae is a classic monotrichous example. It is distinguished from amphitrichous (one flagellum at each of two poles) by involving only a single pole, and from lophotrichous (a tuft at one pole) by carrying only one flagellum rather than a cluster.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amphitrichous describes a single flagellum at each of the cell's two poles (two flagella total, one per end), not one flagellum at only one end.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lophotrichous describes a tuft (group) of several flagella at one pole, not a single flagellum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peritrichous (pertrichate) describes flagella distributed all around the cell, not confined to one end.

questions.learning_objective: Name "monotrichous" as the term for a single flagellum at one pole of a bacterial cell.

questions.title: What a bacterium lacks: a true nucleus
questions.question: A bacterium does not have a?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Every bacterial cell has cytoplasm, the fluid interior in which its ribosomes, nucleoid and metabolic reactions sit.
explanations.B: Correct. A bacterium lacks a true, membrane-bound nucleus -- its DNA is instead held free in the cytoplasm within an unbound region called the nucleoid. This absence of a nuclear envelope is one of the defining features that separates a prokaryotic cell from a eukaryotic one, which does enclose its DNA inside a true nucleus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Protoplasm (the cytoplasm plus its contents, bounded by the plasma membrane) is present in every living bacterial cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A bacterium does have DNA -- a single circular chromosome -- it simply is not enclosed in a nuclear membrane; lacking DNA altogether would mean the cell is not alive.

questions.learning_objective: State that a bacterium lacks a true, membrane-bound nucleus, while still possessing cytoplasm, protoplasm and DNA.

questions.title: Plasma membrane as a selective barrier
questions.question: The plasma membrane is considered a barrier to the environment because?

options.A: Only water and small molecules may penetrate the membrane
options.B: The membrane is the outermost structure of the cell
options.C: It controls the passage of molecules into the cell
options.E: No molecules may pass through it

explanations.A: Incorrect. Restricting passage to only water and small molecules overstates the membrane's selectivity -- many larger molecules and ions cross it too, via specific transport proteins and channels, not just small solutes by simple diffusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In a bacterium the plasma membrane sits internal to the cell wall (and capsule, where present); it is not the cell's outermost structure.
explanations.C: Correct. The plasma membrane is termed a barrier because it selectively controls which molecules pass into and out of the cell, rather than letting everything through freely or blocking everything entirely. This selective-permeability function -- not rigidity, not being the outermost layer, and not total exclusion -- is the defining reason the membrane is described as a barrier to the environment. It achieves this control through the lipid bilayer itself plus embedded transport proteins and channels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The plasma membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer, not a rigid structure; rigidity and shape are instead provided by the cell wall.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The membrane does allow selective passage of molecules (via diffusion, channels and transporters); it does not block all molecules completely, which would make the cell unable to obtain nutrients or excrete waste.

questions.learning_objective: State that the plasma membrane acts as a barrier by selectively controlling molecular passage into and out of the cell, not by rigidity, outer position, or total exclusion.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Where genetic information is stored
questions.question: Where is the genetic information of the cell stored?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The rough endoplasmic reticulum is the site of protein synthesis and folding for secreted and membrane proteins; it does not store the cell's genetic material.
explanations.B: Correct. Among the organelles listed, the nucleus is the one that houses a cell's genetic material (DNA), enclosed within its own nuclear envelope. None of the other three listed structures -- rough ER, Golgi apparatus, or lysosomes -- has any role in storing DNA; each instead handles protein processing, packaging/secretion, or intracellular digestion respectively.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery elsewhere in the cell; it plays no role in storing genetic material.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes for breaking down waste, debris and ingested material; they do not store the cell's genetic material.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the nucleus, among nucleus/rough ER/Golgi/lysosome, as the organelle that stores a cell's genetic material.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Selective barrier regulating cellular traffic
questions.question: What structure acts as a selective barrier, regulating the traffic of materials into and out of the cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cytoskeleton provides internal structural support and enables shape and movement; it does not regulate what crosses into or out of the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nuclear envelope regulates traffic between the nucleus and cytoplasm specifically (via nuclear pores), not traffic between the whole cell and its external environment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The extracellular matrix is the network of material surrounding cells in a tissue, providing structural and biochemical support; it is not itself a selective barrier regulating what enters or leaves an individual cell.
explanations.D: Correct. The plasma membrane is the structure that regulates the traffic of materials into and out of the cell as a whole -- it is a selectively permeable barrier, controlling passage through the lipid bilayer itself and through embedded channel and transport proteins. This whole-cell gatekeeping role is distinct from the nuclear envelope's more limited nucleus-cytoplasm traffic, the cytoskeleton's structural role, and the extracellular matrix's role outside the cell entirely.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the plasma membrane as the structure that selectively regulates material traffic into and out of the whole cell, distinct from the nuclear envelope, cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Lophotrichous flagellar arrangement
questions.question: A group of flagella at one pole of a bacterial cell is known as?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Monotrichous describes a single flagellum at one pole, not a group/tuft of several flagella.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peritrichate (peritrichous) describes flagella distributed all around the cell surface, not clustered at one single pole.
explanations.C: Correct. Lophotrichous describes a tuft (group) of several flagella emerging from one single pole of the bacterial cell. It is distinguished from monotrichous (one flagellum, one pole) by flagellar number, and from amphitrichous (a single flagellum at each of both poles) by involving only one pole. Pseudomonas is a commonly cited example of a lophotrichous organism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amphitrichous (amphitrichate) describes a single flagellum at each of the cell's two poles, not a group clustered at just one pole.

questions.learning_objective: Name "lophotrichous" as the term for a tuft of several flagella at one pole of a bacterial cell.

questions.title: Bacterial virulence factors: the exception
questions.question: Bacterial virulence factors include all EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a genuine virulence factor, so not the EXCEPT answer). Secreted extracellular enzymes help bacteria invade and damage host tissue, a standard virulence mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect (genuine virulence factor). The polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis by host immune cells, a standard antiphagocytic virulence factor.
explanations.C: Incorrect (genuine virulence factor). Pili (fimbriae) mediate bacterial adherence to host cells and surfaces, the first step in establishing many infections.
explanations.D: Incorrect (genuine virulence factor). Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide, released from the Gram-negative outer membrane) triggers inflammatory and septic effects in the host, a standard virulence factor.
explanations.E: Correct. Inclusion granules are intracellular storage deposits (e.g. glycogen, polyphosphate) that a bacterium accumulates as a nutrient reserve for its own metabolism -- they play no direct role in helping the organism invade, damage or evade the host immune system, unlike the capsule, pili, extracellular enzymes and endotoxin listed alongside them. This makes inclusion granules the one listed structure that is not a virulence factor.

questions.learning_objective: List the standard bacterial virulence factors (capsule, pili, extracellular enzymes, endotoxin) and identify inclusion granules as a storage structure, not a virulence factor.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 1, p26

questions.title: Amphitrichous flagellar arrangement
questions.question: How do you describe flagella distributed as a single flagellum in each pole of bacillus?

explanations.A: Correct. Amphitrichous (amphitichous) describes a single flagellum located at each of the cell's two poles -- one flagellum per end, two flagella total. This is distinguished from monotrichous (one flagellum at only one pole) by involving both poles, and from lophotrichous (a tuft at one pole) by carrying only a single flagellum per pole rather than a cluster.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Bitrichous" is not a standard flagellar-arrangement term used in this classification scheme.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Ditrichous" is likewise not a standard term in the monotrichous/amphitrichous/lophotrichous/peritrichous classification scheme.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lophotrichous describes a tuft of several flagella at one single pole, not one flagellum at each of two poles.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Monotrichous describes a single flagellum at only one pole of the cell, not one flagellum at each of both poles.

questions.learning_objective: Name "amphitrichous" as the term for a single flagellum at each of a bacterial cell's two poles.

questions.title: Bacterial spores: the false statement
questions.question: All of the following statement regarding bacterial spores are true EXCEPT?

options.B: Are more resistant than vegetative cells
options.C: Are formed within certain Gram +ve cells

explanations.A: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Bacterial endospores (formed by genera such as Bacillus and Clostridium) are dormant, non-replicating structures with essentially no active metabolism -- their entire biological purpose is to survive harsh conditions in a metabolically inactive state, not to remain metabolically active.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Endospores are highly resistant to heat, desiccation, radiation and chemicals, far more so than the vegetative (actively growing) bacterial cell that formed them.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Endospore formation (sporulation) occurs within certain Gram-positive rods, classically Bacillus and Clostridium species, typically triggered by nutrient limitation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). The dense, resistant spore coat does not take up the Gram stain, so spores appear as unstained, clear/refractile areas within or beside the parent cell on a Gram-stained smear.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that bacterial endospores are metabolically dormant (not active), while correctly being highly resistant, formed within certain Gram-positive rods, and unstained by Gram stain.
